# Photography (`photography`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by camera_obscura, nitric_acid, lenses, achromatic_lens, glassmaking
- Core idea: Some silver salts darken in light. Silver dissolved in nitric acid gives silver nitrate; paper soaked first in weak salt water and then in silver nitrate solution (worked by candlelight) carries silver chloride and turns dark where light falls. Put it in a camera obscura with a lens, or lay a leaf or drawing on it in the sun. The picture must then be fixed, or it blackens all over: wash it in a solution of 'hypo' (sodium thiosulphate), which dissolves the unused silver salt; strong salt water works poorly. Exposure falls from hours to seconds if the invisible latent image is developed chemically (gallic acid on paper, mercury vapour on Daguerre's iodised silver plate). Talbot’s paper negative yields positive contact prints. Each daguerreotype is a unique image on its plate.
- Pitfalls:
  - No fixing step: the image disappears on the first viewing in daylight (Wedgwood's problem in 1802)
  - Not knowing how to make thiosulphate (boil sulphite solution with sulphur)
  - Mercury fumes of the daguerreotype process are poisonous; silver nitrate stains and burns skin
  - Expecting portraits at once: early exposures took minutes to hours
- History: europe: c. 1717–1727 Schulze shows silver salts darken by light, not heat; 1802 Wedgwood and Davy, unfixed images; 1826 or 1827 Niépce's first surviving camera picture (bitumen); 1839 Daguerre and Talbot announce their processes, Herschel introduces hypo; 1841 calotype; 1851 Archer's wet collodion; 1871 Maddox's gelatine dry plate; americas: 1888 – Eastman's roll-film Kodak
- Read:
  - William Henry Fox Talbot, The Pencil of Nature (1844)
  - Helmut Gernsheim with Alison Gernsheim, The History of Photography from the Earliest Use of the Camera Obscura in the Eleventh Century up to 1914 (1955)
